title: Youth wellbeing and civic confidence are tied to local third spaces, trusted adults, affordable opportunity, and whether young people feel heard
source_unit: UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport, Youth Matters: State of the Nation, updated 12 August 2026
geography: England primarily, with selected UK-wide comparisons; young people ages 10-21 and up to 25 for those with special educational needs or disabilities

denominator.unit: young people ages 10-21, up to 25 for those with SEN/D, in the National Youth Strategy Survey in England

concern_set.value: friendships and social life, school or college, money, future plans, and mental health and wellbeing were the five major concern areas

daily_life_priorities.value: young people prioritized lower living costs, more recreational and leisure activities, better mental-health support, secure jobs, and good-quality healthcare

system_link.value: the report connects community, connection and belonging; physical, mental and digital wellbeing; skills and opportunity; and safety and security

uneven_exposure.value: challenges are disproportionately experienced by young people with SEN/D and those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds

observations.method: National Youth Strategy Survey of more than 14,000 young people combined with focus groups, workshops, youth-sector engagement, and youth collaborators.
observations.uncertainty: The report combines primary and secondary evidence across different years and geographies; the priority rankings are descriptive and do not establish one causal hierarchy among youth concerns.
observations.subgroup: Young people ages 10-21, young people with SEN/D up to age 25, lower socioeconomic groups, communities outside London, youth-sector organizations, and local institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Young people’s priorities may shift with local conditions, economic cycles, age, family support, and policy visibility; interconnected problems do not imply one universal intervention.

observations.period: 2025-2026; trusted adults, local belonging, and third spaces

denominator.unit: Youth Matters synthesis of UK youth surveys and community research

trusted_adult_gap.value: around one in five young people ages 13-17 in England and Wales do not have a trusted adult outside their family

loneliness.value: about one third of young people ages 10-19 report feeling alone or lonely some of the time

local_belonging.unit: percent of young people agreeing they feel they belong with people in their local area; 46% among ages 16-25 versus 57% among ages 10-15

youth_facility_spending.unit: percent fall in spending on youth facilities between 2010/11 and 2022/23

third_space_route.value: young people describe youth clubs and free, accessible places outside home and school as spaces for belonging, trusted adults, activities, advice, and safer social connection

observations.method: Cross-source DCMS synthesis combining the National Youth Strategy Survey, youth engagement, youth-sector evidence, and cited UK statistics.
observations.uncertainty: The report’s synthesis spans different data sources and periods; the relationship between youth-facility spending and loneliness or belonging is not a causal estimate.
observations.subgroup: Young people in England and Wales, older adolescents, rural youth, young women, lower-income communities, youth workers, mentors, and local public spaces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital communities, schools, sports, faith groups, libraries, and informal peer networks can provide belonging even where formal youth facilities decline; local provision is heterogeneous.

observations.period: 2025-2026; access to activities and place-based inequality

denominator.unit: National Youth Strategy Survey young people in England; selected activity measures draw on cited DCMS Youth Participation Pilot surveys

activity_sufficiency.unit: percent of young people ages 10-19 agreeing there are enough clubs and activities in their area

local_service_happiness.unit: percent agreeing they are happy with activities and services in their local area

local_fit.unit: percent agreeing local activities and services are made for young people like them

fun_access_priority.unit: percent selecting more recreational and leisure activities as something that would most improve daily life

access_gradient.value: satisfaction and participation are lower for some lower socioeconomic groups and young people with SEN/D, while affordability, transport, awareness, and safety shape access

observations.method: National Youth Strategy Survey and cited DCMS youth participation evidence, with qualitative engagement on local activities, transport, affordability, and safety.
observations.uncertainty: Measures combine different surveys and activity universes; reported local satisfaction does not identify whether the constraint is supply, price, transport, awareness, safety, or fit.
observations.subgroup: Young people ages 10-19, older youth, lower-income groups, young people with SEN/D, young women, ethnic-minority groups, rural communities, and local youth services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low reported access may reflect information gaps rather than absence of provision in some places; expanding facilities without transport, affordability, or trusted staffing may not improve participation.

denominator.unit: National Youth Strategy Survey young people in England, with UK electoral and opinion comparisons

voice_matter.value: 49 percent of young people felt negatively about their voice mattering in decisions across the country, compared with 26 percent who agreed

local_influence.value: young people were equally likely to disagree and agree that they know how to influence local decisions, at 34 percent each

electoral_participation.unit: estimated turnout among UK 18-24 year olds in the 2024 general election, compared with 55% among ages 45-54

volunteering_social_action.value: 44 percent of young people ages 10-19 volunteered in the prior year and 47 percent participated in social action; improving the local area was the most common social-action activity

civic_route.value: low formal political confidence coexists with local volunteering, petitions, campaigning, and demand for meaningful youth voice

observations.method: National Youth Strategy Survey combined with electoral participation estimates and cited youth participation and social-action surveys.
observations.uncertainty: Turnout, influence perceptions, volunteering, and social action use different samples and definitions; low electoral participation does not mean absence of civic activity.
observations.subgroup: Young people ages 10-25, young women, ethnic-minority groups, lower-income communities, young people with SEN/D, local authorities, schools, and youth organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived voice can improve through informal or local channels even when national institutions remain distant; formal participation may also be constrained by age, registration, housing mobility, or political supply.

related_sources.claim: The companion National Youth Strategy translates the State of the Nation evidence into policy priorities.
The companion online-wellbeing report provides more detailed evidence on youth digital life, platform design, AI, and safety preferences.

boundary: This record adds UK public research on youth belonging, trusted adults, local third spaces, activity access, economic insecurity, and civic voice. It combines survey, cited secondary, qualitative, and youth-advisory evidence without treating them as one dataset; it is not respondent-level ingestion, a causal evaluation of youth services, a global youth estimate, or proof that any single investment reverses wellbeing or turnout patterns.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GOV.UK Youth Matters page reviewed for survey frame, youth priorities, trusted-adult and loneliness context, youth-facility spending, local activity access, belonging, civic voice, participation, and subgroup differences.
